title: KS2 GPS terminology
examples: When do I use a fronted adverbial?
What is the difference between 'can' and 'could'?
Can you show me where to put a determiner?

explain.say: Today we are learning about three grammar tools. These help us make our writing more interesting. Our first tool is the fronted adverbial. This is a group of words that starts a sentence.
A fronted adverbial tells us when or where something happens. For example, yesterday, the cat slept all day long. The words yesterday tell us when.

draw.text: Yesterday, the cat slept all day.

explain.say: Next we look at modal verbs. These verbs help us talk about possibility or ability. Modal verbs include words like can, could, might, and will.
A modal verb changes the meaning of the main verb. For instance, you can swim, means you have the ability to swim. You could swim means it is possible.
Our last tool is the determiner. Determiners go before a noun to give more detail. They tell us which specific thing we are talking about.
Look at this sentence. The determiner 'our' tells us whose pencil it is. The fronted adverbial 'After school' tells us when. The modal verb 'should' helps us give advice.

draw.text: After school, we should use our pencils.

faq.q: What is the difference between a determiner and an adjective?
faq.a: A determiner always comes before a noun. An adjective describes the noun but does not have to come first. For example, 'red car' uses an adjective, but 'this car' uses a determiner.
asks: Where do determiners go in a sentence?
Can I use 'my' or 'your' as an adjective?

faq.q: Can I use a fronted adverbial if I start with a conjunction?
faq.a: No, a fronted adverbial usually starts with an adverb or a phrase of time or place. Conjunctions like 'and' connect two ideas together.
asks: Does the adverbial need a comma after it?
What counts as a fronted adverbial?

faq.q: Do I always need a comma after a fronted adverbial?
faq.a: Yes, if the fronted adverbial is a whole phrase, you usually need a comma after it. This helps the reader pause correctly.
asks: Is a comma always needed after an adverbial?
When is a comma optional after an adverbial?

faq.q: What is the difference between 'can' and 'will'?
faq.a: Can often talks about ability right now. Will usually talks about something that will happen in the future. For example, 'I can run' versus 'I will run tomorrow.'
asks: When should I use 'could' instead of 'can'?
Do modal verbs change the tense?

faq.a: Some common determiners are 'the', 'a', 'an', 'this', 'that', and possessives like 'my' and 'your'. They point out which noun we mean.
asks: Do articles like 'a' and 'the' count as determiners?

facts: Fronted adverbials often start a sentence and are followed by a comma.
Modal verbs are helping verbs that change the meaning of the main verb.
Determiners specify or point out a noun, such as 'this' or 'some'.
The word 'might' suggests a possibility, which is less certain than 'will'.

quiz.say: She speak French when she was young.
quiz.show: She speak French when she was young.
quiz.why: We use 'could' to talk about an ability in the past, which fits the phrase 'when she was young.'

wrong.0: Using 'must' suggests a strong necessity, which is too strong for a past ability.
wrong.2: Using 'can' suggests the ability is true right now, not in the past.
wrong.3: Using 'will' suggests a future action, which does not fit the past time frame.

quiz.say: Look at pencil; it is mine.
quiz.show: Look at pencil; it is mine.
quiz.why: We use the determiner 'this' because we are pointing to a specific, nearby pencil.

wrong.0: Using 'a' suggests any pencil, but we are pointing to one specific one.
wrong.1: While 'my' is a determiner, 'this' is better here because it points to the object's location.
wrong.3: This is the noun itself; we need a word to point out which pencil.
